analysis.one_liner: Requires airlines to include one checked bag, carry-on, water, and a seat in ticket prices.
analysis.headline: The bill was introduced in November 2011 and referred to the Senate Commerce Committee, where it died without action, with no cosponsors.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have directed the FAA to write rules requiring airlines to let every ticketed passenger check one bag and carry on a personal item and a carry-on bag without extra fees, and to give passengers on board access to a seat, water, and bathrooms. Airlines that broke the rules would face civil penalties. The bill never received a hearing, a committee vote, or a floor vote.
analysis.who_benefits: Air travelers who now pay $25 or more per checked bag and face carry-on fees on some discount carriers. Any passenger who has been charged separately for a bag would keep that money in their pocket. Passengers on ultra-low-cost carriers, whose fees hit budget travelers hardest, would see the biggest savings.

how_it_helps.text: Bars airlines from charging a separate fee for the first checked bag or a basic carry-on, folding those into the ticket price [S2] [S3].
Guarantees every boarded passenger access to a seat, drinking water, and bathroom facilities, with civil penalties on airlines that fail to comply [S2] [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Airlines would lose the baggage-fee revenue, which industry-wide runs into the billions of dollars a year. Some of the cost could be passed back into slightly higher base fares, but the fee would no longer surprise passengers at checkout.

drawbacks.text: Requiring a free checked bag could raise base ticket prices for everyone, including travelers who carry everything aboard and today pay nothing extra [S3].
Overweight and oversized baggage would still be chargeable under the airline's existing policy, so the guarantee only covers standard-size items [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefits are real but modest in dollars per traveler, while the cost falls on an industry earning billions in ancillary fees; the trade-off is essentially moving airline revenue from hidden fees into the visible fare. One honest objection is that bundling a free checked bag could nudge base fares up for carry-on-only travelers. The core consumer protections—water, a seat, bathroom access—are unobjectionable.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the Senate Commerce Committee on the day it was introduced and never received a hearing, a vote, or floor consideration before the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Introduced November 18, 2011 by Senator Mary Landrieu and referred to the Committee on Commerce, Science, and Transportation the same day [S1] [S5].
No cosponsors ever joined, and the committee took no further action before the 112th Congress ended on January 3, 2013 [S4] [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Airlines, which kept charging separate baggage and carry-on fees with no federal requirement to fold them into ticket prices.

for.name: Sen. Mary Landrieu
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and referred it to the Commerce Committee; no cosponsors joined.

against.name: Senate Commerce, Science, and Transportation Committee
against.what_they_did: Took no action on the bill after referral; no hearing, markup, or vote was scheduled.

against.name: U.S. airline industry
against.what_they_did: Had a direct financial stake in keeping baggage and carry-on fees outside the ticket price; the bill would have imposed civil penalties for charging them.

sides.party_line_note: The bill had a single Democratic sponsor, no cosponsors, and never reached a vote, so no party split appears in the record.

industries.note: The bill would have eliminated first-checked-bag and carry-on fees, revenue streams worth billions of dollars a year industry-wide, and imposed civil penalties for noncompliance. Because the bill died in committee, airlines kept charging these fees. Their interest in keeping the fees ran against travelers who pay them.
